questions.question: What complication do 'time zones' add to clock reasoning?
options: The same instant in time can correspond to different local clock readings depending on location
None — time zones don't affect clock reasoning
They only affect the date, never the time
They only matter for digital clocks
questions.rationale: Time zones mean a single absolute instant can be read as a different local clock time depending on where you are, which must be accounted for in cross-location problems.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'absolute' and 'local' time?
options: There is no real difference
Absolute time only applies to GMT
Absolute time is a fixed, location-independent reference point; local time is that same instant expressed according to a specific time zone's offset
Local time is always 12 hours ahead of absolute time
questions.rationale: Absolute time is a single, location-independent reference; local time is that same instant re-expressed using a particular location's time zone offset.

questions.question: What does 'temporal precision' refer to?
options: The exact brand of the clock used
The level of detail (e.g., to the second, minute, or hour) at which a time value is specified or required
Whether a clock is analog or digital
The angle between the clock hands
questions.rationale: Temporal precision describes how finely a time is specified or needed — down to the second, the minute, or only the hour, for instance.

questions.question: What is an 'uncertainty interval' in clock reasoning?
options: A malfunctioning clock
A fixed 60-minute block
The interval between AM and PM
A range of possible times, used when the exact time isn't precisely known or stated
questions.rationale: An uncertainty interval represents a range of possible times when the exact value isn't precisely known, rather than forcing a single (possibly wrong) exact answer.

questions.question: What is the purpose of stating a set of 'core rules' late in a lesson like this?
options: To consolidate the many individual concepts covered into a short, memorable checklist for quick reference
To introduce entirely new material
To replace the need for the earlier sections
To make the lesson longer without adding value
questions.rationale: A late-lesson core-rules summary condenses everything covered so far into a compact, quickly-reviewable checklist rather than requiring a full re-read.

questions.question: What does a 'minimal algorithm' for clock reasoning aim to provide?
options: The most complicated possible solution
A shortcut that skips verification entirely
The smallest consistent set of steps needed to solve any standard clock reasoning problem, stripped of unnecessary detail
A method that only works for one specific problem
questions.rationale: A minimal algorithm distills the reasoning process down to the smallest consistent set of steps that reliably solves any standard problem in the domain.

questions.question: Why work through a 'complete multi-step example' near the end of a lesson?
options: It has no pedagogical value
To show how all the individual rules and steps combine to solve a realistic, non-trivial problem end-to-end
To replace the need for the core rules summary
Because simple examples are no longer useful at this stage
questions.rationale: A complete multi-step example demonstrates how everything taught throughout the lesson comes together to solve a realistic problem from start to finish.

questions.question: What is 'the deeper principle' this lesson points to as the real skill being tested?
options: Memorizing every possible clock question
That time zones are the only truly important topic
That only the clock-angle formula matters
That clock reasoning is fundamentally about consistent unit conversion and modular arithmetic, not memorized tricks
questions.rationale: The lesson's recurring theme is that reliable clock reasoning comes from consistently applying unit conversion and modular arithmetic, not from memorizing isolated tricks.

questions.question: Why must time zone conversions account for more than just adding/subtracting a fixed offset in some real-world cases?
options: They never need more than a fixed offset
Because factors like daylight saving time can change the offset depending on the date
Because time zones don't actually have offsets
Because local time never differs from absolute time
questions.rationale: Daylight saving time and similar seasonal adjustments mean a time zone's offset from a reference time can change depending on the date, not just the location.

questions.question: When precision is lower than what a question requires (e.g., only the hour is known but minutes are needed), what should a careful reasoner do?
options: Assume the minutes are always zero
Acknowledge the missing precision rather than assuming an exact but unstated value
Guess a random minute value
Refuse to answer any part of the question
questions.rationale: Rather than silently assuming an unstated value (which could be wrong), a careful reasoner should acknowledge that the available precision doesn't support a fully exact answer.
